The drag force is modeled as proportional to the square of velocity, and the study examines how this nonlinear effect impacts WEC dynamics by sweeping wave heights from 1–4 m, periods from 4–16 s, and biofouling protrusion from 0 to 0.1 m. The simulation results demonstrate that biofouling has significant and quantifiable effects on WEC performance. At H=2 m and the resonant period of 12 seconds, average PTO power decreases by 15% when biofouling reaches k=0.1 m, while peak velocity and displacement decrease by approximately 10%. The study also reveals that optimal damping conditions shift with biofouling: as roughness increases, both the optimal period and optimal damping coefficient decrease. For example, at H=2 m, the optimal damping drops from 12,000 kN/m/s with no biofouling to 9,602 kN/m/s at k=0.1 m—a 20% reduction. Importantly, the power reduction effects are more dramatic at higher wave heights, with losses becoming increasingly severe as H increases from 1 m to 4 m. The authors examine whether adjusting control parameters can recover lost power due to biofouling. They find that re-tuning the PTO damping to the new optimal value for k=0.1 m recovers only about 2 kW, representing no more than 6% of the overall power reduction—indicating that biofouling's physical effects dominate over what control adjustments can compensate. The paper notes that while anti-fouling coatings require impractical yearly application, a more practical approach may be to set the PTO damping to optimal values for expected maximum biofouling levels after initial deployment years. The authors also note that biofouling affects factors beyond drag, such as added mass from organisms like mussels (40 kg/m²), which could increase the RM3's mass by over 7% if fully covered, potentially creating additional performance impacts not captured in this drag-focused study. 6 The Barton, Brekken, and Cao paper presents a reinforcement learning approach to maximize power generation from marine hydrokinetic turbines (HKTs) while accounting for the degrading effects of biofouling. The authors address a key challenge for marine energy adoption: high levelized cost of energy (LCOE), which can be reduced by maximizing energy extraction. The paper develops a SARSA (state- action-reward-state-action) algorithm using Gaussian radial basis functions for function approximation, which learns the optimal damping coefficient to apply to a direct-drive 5 kW turbine based on incoming flow velocity. The HKT model is derived from experimental data, and biofouling effects are characterized using a logistic growth model that predicts 100% surface coverage in approximately 400 days for calcareous fouling (barnacles, mussels). The biofouling shifts the Cp versus TSR curve, reducing maximum Cp by 0.08 and shifting optimal TSR downward by 0.7. The RL framework uses flow velocity as the state, damping coefficient as the action, and coefficient of power (Cp) as the reward signal. The agent employs an ε-greedy policy for balancing exploration and exploitation, with exploration constrained to within 5 Nm·s/rad of the current damping coefficient to prevent damaging torque spikes.
